newsitem.title: FRANCE: Train carrying spent nuclear fuel derails in France.
newsitem.headline: Train carrying spent nuclear fuel derails in France.

text.p: A train carrying spent nuclear fuel came off the rails in eastern France close to the border with Germany and Luxembourg on Tuesday but there was no radiation leak, French and German officials said.

"A locomotive coming from Germany en route to Britain was derailed at Apach, near the border at Schengen. There was radioactive material aboard but there are no leaks," a spokeswoman for the prefect's office for France's Moselle department told Reuters by telephone from Metz.

An official in the Apach city hall said the accident had occurred just outside the village of 800 people, on a rail line running alongside the Moselle river. The site is about 500 metres (yards) from the border.
Officials said they decided against evacuating residents as there was no danger. But emergency workers sealed off the immediate area as a routine precautionary measure.
German officials said 60 to 80 nuclear convoys a year travel through Germany each year.

Germany's opposition Greens party said the accident was one of a series of recent nuclear mishaps including an incident at Britain's Sellafield plant on Sunday in which six workers were contaminated by radioactive dust.

"These incidents are the logical consequence of a policy which consistently ignores the incalculable risks of atomic energy to both people and the environment,and focuses on economic interests," the party said in a statement.
The convoy was carrying 18 spent fuel elements from the Lingen power station in Lower Saxony, according to the Lower Saxony environment ministry.
A statement from the prefect's office in Metz said the convoy belonging to British Nuclear Fuels PLC and was on its way to Dunkirk for shipment to Britain by ferry.

The train consisted of a locomotive and three wagons, each carrying radioactive materials in British ''Excellox 6" protective containers, German and French officials said. The containers each weigh 94 tonnes fully charged, French nuclear safety experts said.
Officials said the first wagon towed by the locomotive was leaning over after the accident while the second remained upright and the third had partially left the rails.
Emergency teams at the site measured no unusual radiation and observed no leaks around the wagons, the statement said.
The officials said two of the three wagons would be put back on the rails while the cargo on the third would be shifted to a new wagon. They said this would take about 24 hours.
The Saarland state Interior Ministry said the shipment was on its way to the reprocessing plant at Sellafield.
"Nothing has fallen over, nothing dramatic has happened, it's just a derailment," ministry spokesman Christian Petry said.
Petry said the Saarland situation centre first learned at 6.40 a.m. (0540 GMT) that a train with radioactive material had been derailed.
First indications were that the cause may have been a broken rail or a sleeper too weak for the weight of train.
